answers.answer: A shared file service exposes named files and filesystem operations such as open, read, update, rename and close. Files hold bytes; directories organize names into paths, and metadata describes size, owner and permissions. The service manages the shared filesystem. Blocks expose addressed blocks, objects expose keys, and databases add records, field queries and transaction rules. Mounting attaches access to a filesystem at a local directory: /shared/report.csv can reach a remote file without copying the dataset or formatting a client disk. A read goes from the program to the operating system's filesystem client, which can use cached data or send a remote request across the network to the service and return the result. EFS uses NFS, Network File System, for remote operations; its mount target is the service's network endpoint. A compatible client, reachable endpoint and authorized access are required.

evidence.quote: A file holds bytes under a name. Directories organize those names into paths, such as /assets/logo.svg. Metadata describes a file: its size, owner and access permissions. A shared file service maintains this filesystem and accepts file operations from multiple hosts.

Applications open, read, update, rename and close files through a filesystem interface. The service manages the shared file organization; each client does not independently manage the same raw disk structures.

A block device exposes addressed blocks. Object storage exposes objects by key. A database adds records, field queries and transaction rules. Shared files provide neither a raw block attachment nor automatic database transactions.

Mounting makes a filesystem accessible at a directory in a host's local path tree. After mounting a share at /shared, a program can open /shared/report.csv using its usual file operations. This does not copy the dataset to the host or require formatting a client disk.

The program calls the operating system. Its filesystem client sends needed requests across the network to the file service and returns results to the program. Some requests can use a client cache, a local copy kept to avoid another network trip.

NFS means Network File System, a protocol for remote file operations. Amazon EFS uses NFS. An EFS mount target is a network endpoint through which clients reach the filesystem. A compatible client, a reachable endpoint and authorized access are all needed; a familiar path does not remove those dependencies.

answers.answer: A buffered write may report success while bytes remain in volatile client memory, so a client crash can lose data the service never received. EFS close-to-open consistency means a later opener can see changes after a writer finishes and successfully closes; it does not promise immediate freshness to an already-open reader. For durability, forward application-held buffers, await required flush or close and check errors using the supported completion procedure. fsync cannot forward private application buffers. EFS documents Regional writes stored across Availability Zones at successful synchronous completion, such as fsync, or file close. The counter increment is lost because two successful writes of 11 do not make the read-compute-write operations indivisible. A single writer can serialize updates, or all participants can acquire a supported lock before reading and hold it over the entire read-modify-write sequence through required writes. Locking only the write leaves stale reads. EFS advisory locks require cooperation and do not stop an ignoring program from accessing data. Locks cannot undo a partial update after a crash. Several related files changing together need application or database transactions and recovery that recovers the complete update rather than an arbitrary subset.

evidence.quote: A client can cache file contents and metadata, and buffer pending writes in volatile memory. An ordinary buffered write can succeed before its bytes reach the service. A client crash can lose those bytes; remote persistent storage cannot preserve data it never received.

EFS provides close-to-open consistency: after a writer finishes writing and successfully closes, a later opener can see the changes. This is not a promise that an already-open reader immediately sees every concurrent write. Follow the client and service's documented cache rules.

Ask when the service has safely stored the bytes. Use the supported completion procedure, including sending application-held buffers onward, awaiting the required flush or close and checking errors. fsync is a file synchronization operation; it cannot send bytes still held only in an application's private buffer.

EFS documents storage across Availability Zones for Regional filesystem writes at successful synchronous completion, such as fsync, or file close. An Availability Zone is an isolated infrastructure location within a cloud Region. This durability boundary does not make several writes a transaction or protect them from later deletion.

Suppose two clients each read a counter of 10, compute 11 and write 11. Both file writes can succeed, yet the final value is 11 rather than 12. The filesystem performed the individual operations; it did not make each read-compute-write sequence one indivisible update.

A single writer can process updates in order. Alternatively, every participant can use a supported lock, a coordination rule that reserves access while an update runs. Acquire it before reading, protect the entire read-modify-write sequence and release it after completing the required writes. Locking only the final write leaves the stale-read problem.

EFS locks are advisory: a program that ignores the lock can still read or write. All participants must cooperate with the same supported locking protocol. Sharing a directory alone does not provide that cooperation.

A lock also cannot undo half an update after a crash. When several related files must change together, use an application or database transaction and recovery design. Atomic recovery means related changes can be recovered as a complete update rather than an arbitrary subset.

answers.answer: Network reachability and client authorization to use EFS are separate from file and directory permissions, so mounting can succeed while a write is denied. EFS uses Unix-style ownership and permissions with numeric user and group IDs. Read permits reading contents and write permits modifying them. Directory execute/search permission permits traversal to a path beneath that directory. Matching usernames with different numeric IDs are different identities to EFS. Check effective IDs sent by the client, file ownership, group membership, required directory permissions and client policy; align intended identities and grant only needed access. Making the share writable by everyone conceals the cause and permits unrelated clients to damage data.

evidence.quote: Network rules determine whether the client can reach the service. Client authorization determines whether it may use the filesystem; EFS can use IAM, AWS's identity and access-management policies, when configured. File and directory permissions still control access inside it. A successful mount can therefore be followed by a denied write.

EFS uses Unix-style ownership and permissions with numeric user IDs and group IDs. Read permission allows reading file contents; write permission allows modifying them. A directory's execute, or search, permission allows traversal through that directory to a path beneath it.

The same username on two hosts can map to different numeric IDs. EFS then sees different identities, despite the matching name. Check the effective IDs sent by the client, file ownership, group membership, required directory permissions and client policy.
Align the intended identities and grant only the access the application needs. Making the whole share writable by everyone hides the diagnosis and grants unrelated clients permission to damage data.

answers.answer: Availability is access now; durability is retention of stored data. Losing the network route can prevent remote file requests from progressing even with every byte retained. NFS hard mounts retry timed-out requests until the server responds, so application I/O can wait. Soft timeouts return errors and interrupt operations, introducing data-integrity risks; use supported settings and plan application behavior for unavailable storage. An Availability Zone is an isolated infrastructure location within a Region. Regional EFS stores data across multiple zones; One Zone stores within one and can lose data in a zone disaster. Redundancy does not fix clients or network paths, and cannot undo authorized deletion or bad writes. The application also needs working clients, reachable endpoints and a recovery plan.

evidence.quote: Availability means being able to access data now. Durability concerns retaining stored data. If a host loses its network route, remote file requests can stop progressing even when the service still has every byte.

With an NFS hard mount, timed-out requests keep retrying until the server responds. Application I/O can wait during an outage. Switching to soft timeouts is not a harmless responsiveness fix: returned errors and interrupted operations can introduce data-integrity risks. Follow supported mount settings and design how the application handles unavailable storage.

EFS documents storage across Availability Zones for Regional filesystem writes at successful synchronous completion, such as fsync, or file close. An Availability Zone is an isolated infrastructure location within a cloud Region. This durability boundary does not make several writes a transaction or protect them from later deletion.

Check the actual failure boundary. EFS Regional stores data across multiple Availability Zones; EFS One Zone stores it within one zone and can lose data in a zone disaster. The generic file-storage interface does not imply either placement.

Storage redundancy does not repair a broken client or network path, and it does not undo an authorized deletion or bad write. The application needs working clients, reachable service endpoints and a recovery plan as well as redundant storage.

answers.answer: Redundancy retains copies of current state, so a mistaken overwrite can be copied too. A useful backup schedule and retention period preserve earlier usable history until damage is discovered. A live EFS backup is not necessarily an atomic application snapshot: writes, renames, moves or deletes can make related files reflect different update stages. Use the application's supported backup procedure, coordinate pending writes and pause modifying processes when required or use a period without modifications. Pausing new work does not flush application-memory buffers. Restore an appropriate recovery point to a controlled destination, verify files, permissions and application behavior, and measure recovery time. Set backup frequency and retention based on tolerable lost work and downtime; backup-job success alone does not establish a usable restore.

evidence.quote: Redundancy preserves copies of the current state, including a mistaken overwrite. Recovery from that mistake needs an earlier backup. Set a backup schedule and retention period that leave usable history when damage is discovered.

A live file backup is not automatically an atomic application snapshot. AWS warns that writes, renames, moves or deletes during an EFS backup can leave inconsistent results. Related files may reflect different stages of an application update.

Use the application's supported backup procedure. Coordinate pending writes and pause modifying processes for the backup when required, or choose a period with no modifications. Pausing new work alone does not flush bytes still held in application memory.

Restore a suitable recovery point to a controlled destination. Check files, permissions and application behavior, and measure the recovery time. Choose backup frequency and retention around how much work you can afford to lose and how long you can be down. A successful backup job alone does not prove a usable restore.

answers.answer: Capacity is stored bytes, throughput bytes transferred per second, IOPS operations per second, and latency time per operation. Tiny-file open, lookup and close operations add metadata work and network round trips for little data; larger reads spread overhead across more bytes. More clients can improve independent work, but contenders on one file lock may simply wait longer. Measure representative operation sizes and mix, metadata activity, latency, aggregate throughput and lock waits; inspect client, network and service limits before adding performance or parallelism. Shared files fit several hosts requiring existing pathname operations over files and directories. Block storage fits a raw disk-like device; object storage fits blobs retrieved by key; databases fit record queries and transactions. Before putting a database on shared files, verify that its engine supports the filesystem's locking, durability and recovery behavior. Pointing multiple database processes at one directory does not create a safe multi-writer database. Managed service administration does not remove application coordination, identity and permissions, network access, performance choices or tested recovery responsibilities.

evidence.quote: Capacity measures stored bytes. Throughput measures bytes transferred per second. IOPS counts input/output operations per second. Latency is the time one operation takes. Increasing capacity does not by itself promise faster access.

Opening, looking up and closing tiny files adds metadata work and network round trips for little useful data. Metadata work manages names and file attributes rather than transferring the file's contents. Larger reads can spread that overhead over more bytes, so equal byte counts need not take equal time.

Additional clients can help independent work. They do not remove a bottleneck where all updates wait for the same file's lock; more contenders may simply wait longer. This competition for a shared resource is contention.

Measure a representative workload: operation sizes and mix, metadata activity, latency, aggregate throughput and lock waits. Check client, network and service limits before increasing provisioned performance or parallelism. Change the part that limits the workload rather than assuming more storage or more hosts will help.
Fits several hosts that need existing pathname-based operations over files and directories through a supported filesystem interface.

Use block storage for a disk-like device, object storage for blobs retrieved by key, and a database for record queries and transactions. These can be layers in one design rather than competing replacements.

A database may keep its own files on shared storage only when it supports the chosen filesystem's locking, durability and recovery behavior. Several database processes pointed at one directory do not automatically form a safe multi-writer database. Check the engine's requirements before choosing that layout.

A managed file service can remove file-server administration. Application coordination, identities and permissions, network access, workload performance and tested recovery still need deliberate choices. Match those responsibilities to the workload before selecting the service.
